title: トランプ氏 選挙遊説巡り二転三転
body: 【ワシントン時事】トランプ米大統領は30日、ホワイトハウスで記者団に、11月3日の中間選挙前最後の週末に中西部アイオワ、カンザス両州で演説すると明らかにした。【ひと目でわかる】米中間選挙の情勢いったんは両州で予定していた選挙集会に代わり電話を通じて投票を促す「電話集会」に切り替えたが、再び方針を転換し現地入りする。トランプ氏は、遊説日程が二転三転した理由について「電話集会で対応できるか試してみたかった。非常に成功しているからだ」と指摘。ただ、地元関係者から訪問を要請されたため、11月1日に両州を訪れることにしたと説明した。両州は共和党の牙城だが、上院選ではいずれも同党候補が接戦を強いられている。トランプ氏の支持率が低迷する中、選挙情勢に影響が及ぶのを避けるために集会を取りやめたのではないかとの臆測も出ていた。

title: 発達障害増加 支援学校の教員不足
body:
障害児らが通う特別支援学校で、教員不足が深刻化している。文部科学省が今年公表した調査結果では、教員の定数に対する不足人数の割合（不足率）は直近４年間で３倍近くに増加した。発達障害のある子どもが増えていることが背景にある。石川県では今年６月、授業中に行方不明になった男子児童が死亡する事故も起き、専門家が早急な対応を訴えている。（広瀬航太郎）【図】一目でわかる…発達障害の主なタイプと特性
石川県小松市の県立小松特別支援学校で今年６月、５年生の男子児童（当時１０歳）が授業中にトイレに行こうと席を立ったまま行方不明になり、翌日に約１キロ離れた滝で死亡しているのが見つかった。
「突発で何かがあった時に対応できる人員が十分ではない」。塩田憲司・県教育長は７月の記者会見で、そう語った。県は９月、特別支援学校５校で校内を循環する「見守りスタッフ」を新たに９人配置した。
文科省が今年公表した実態調査によると、全国の特別支援学校に配置されている教員数は、昨年５月時点で８万２３２０人。定数に対して５８９人不足しており、「不足率」は０・７１％となった。５年前は７万８６３２人の定数に対して不足は２０５人（不足率０・２６％）で、３倍近くに増加したことになる。小中高校でも教員は不足しているが、特別支援学校は各割合と比べても大きく上回っている。
背景には、発達障害と診断される子どもの増加がある。２０２２年の厚生労働省の調査によると、発達障害と診断された１８歳未満は３４万人（推計）に上り、１１年から２・５倍に増えた。
増加の要因について、国立成育医療研究センターは、発達障害の認知度が高まり、保護者が子どもを受診させるケースが増えたことを挙げる。特に近年は５歳児健診の普及が全国で進み、障害の特性を早期に把握し、就学前から必要な支援につなげる動きが広がっているという。
特別支援学校に通う児童生徒数も増え続けており、今年５月現在で過去最多の１６万３０００人に達した。

title: 東京メトロ 29年3月値上げ目指す
body: 東京メトロは30日、値上げを含めた運賃改定について、2029年3月の実施を目指していることを明らかにした。【動画でも】リニア中央新幹線、乗り心地は？座席は？荷物は？東京メトロの運賃改定は、消費税の引き上げに伴う改定などを除くと、1995年以来になるという。改定幅は未定で、27年8月以降に国が示す運賃改定の基準をもとに、改定額を検討して申請する。東京メトロの担当者は「大規模浸水対策などの設備投資に充てていきたい」としている。東京メトロは4月、物価や労務費の上昇を背景に、安全性向上のための設備投資などのために運賃改定を検討していると発表していた。（吉田貴司）

title: 列車とクマ衝突 乗客は車内で一夜
body:
10月30日夜、JR宗谷線の特急列車がクマと衝突しました。クマが車両の下に巻き込まれている可能性があるため動けず、乗客は車両内で一夜を明かしました。{ヒグマ画像 2026 秋}また、その後の調べで、先頭車両が脱線していたことがわかりました。事故があったのはJR宗谷線の天塩中川と問寒別駅の間の区間です。30日午後10時50分ごろ、旭川発稚内駅行きの特急サロベツ3号（4両編成）が線路上にいたクマと衝突しました。列車の乗客32人と複数の乗員にケガ人はなく、夜間も列車内には電気が通り暖房は稼働していて、トイレも使用できる状態だということです。JRによりますと、クマが車両の下に巻き込まれ、夜間で確認作業ができず、ハンターの出動を待つため、乗客らは車内で一夜を明かしました。夜が明けた31日午前6時30分ごろからハンター同行のもとで調査を行ったところ、車両の下にクマを巻き込んでいるのが見つかり、先頭車両の1軸目の車輪が進行方向右側に脱線していることが確認されました。
乗客・乗務員にけがはなく、現場に留まっていた乗客32人はタクシーで目的地へ向かいました。この脱線事故の影響で、JR宗谷線は以下の区間で影響が出ています。・音威子府～稚内間：始発から終日運転見合わせ・音威子府～名寄間：一部列車が運休

title: 3歳妹殺害され 3人の兄抱えた思い
body: 2011年3月3日、熊本市のスーパーにあるトイレで3歳の清水心（ここ）ちゃんが大学生の男（当時20）に殺害された。【写真で見る】講演する清水真夕さん　亡くなった心ちゃんと兄たち　心ちゃんの遺体が発見された水路心ちゃんの遺体は近くの水路に遺棄された。大学生だった男は無期懲役の判決が確定している。母親の清水真夕さんは、2026年10月16日、佐賀県吉野ヶ里町の三田川中学校で開かれた「命の大切さを学ぶ教室」で講演をした。娘がいなくなった夜、遺体となった心ちゃんとの対面、母として自分を鼓舞し続けた日々を、生徒たちの前で語った。心ちゃんには3人の兄がいる。清水さんは、息子たちが抱え続けた思いについても語った。※清水真夕さんの講演は全4話で掲載しています。【最初から読む】「この世に地獄があるなら、あの夜は地獄だった」スーパーのトイレで殺害された3歳の娘と犯人が真横を…「見つけることも、捕まえることもできませんでした」【娘を奪われた母の言葉(1)】■1番に「学校に戻る」言った長男　「私はこの子は強いなと思っていました」清水さんは、息子たちについての話を始めた。清水真夕さん「3人の兄たちも、妹を助けられなかったと。実は同じ思いを抱いて成長していきました。事件があったとき、長男は中学1年生でした。皆さんと同じ中学生でした。次男が小学2年生、三男は5歳。保育園の年中さんでした」長男は、事件の後、真っ先に動いた。清水真夕さん「長男はそんな中、1番に『学校に戻る』と言って、学校に戻りました。弟たちの通る道を作ってくれました。長男は苦しいとか悲しいとか、一言も弱音を吐きませんでした。私はこの子は強いなと思っていました」■突然聞こえなくなった長男の左耳「娘の命だけじゃなくて、長男の耳も守れなかった」異変は、事件から2年後に現れた。清水真夕さん「事件から2年経った高校1年生になった時に、長男は耳が聞こえなくなりました。突然聞こえなくなりました。幸い片方の耳は聞こえているんですが、いまだに左耳の聴力が全くなくて、ただ、そのことも『耳が2個あって良かったわ』と笑っていました」清水さんは、そのとき初めて知ったことがあるという。清水真夕さん「子どもはこういう事件があったときとか、親に心配をかけてはいけないと思って、自分がつらいとか、学校でこういうことがあったとか、言わないものなんだと、私はそのときに初めて知りました」そして、改めて悔いを口にした。清水真夕さん「娘の命だけじゃなくて、私は長男の耳も守れなかった。すごく、なんで話を聞いてあげられなかったのかと、すごく後悔しています」

title: トランプ氏 選挙遊説巡り二転三転
body: 【ワシントン時事】トランプ米大統領は30日、ホワイトハウスで記者団に、11月3日の中間選挙前最後の週末に中西部アイオワ、カンザス両州で演説すると明らかにした。【ひと目でわかる】米中間選挙の情勢いったんは両州で予定していた選挙集会に代わり電話を通じて投票を促す「電話集会」に切り替えたが、再び方針を転換し現地入りする。トランプ氏は、遊説日程が二転三転した理由について「電話集会で対応できるか試してみたかった。非常に成功しているからだ」と指摘。ただ、地元関係者から訪問を要請されたため、11月1日に両州を訪れることにしたと説明した。両州は共和党の牙城だが、上院選ではいずれも同党候補が接戦を強いられている。トランプ氏の支持率が低迷する中、選挙情勢に影響が及ぶのを避けるために集会を取りやめたのではないかとの臆測も出ていた。

title: 中間選挙 民主党「赤い州」で勢い
body: 赤をシンボル色とする米与党共和党の牙城「赤い州」の代表格、南部テキサス州が、中間選挙の「天王山」と目される激戦の舞台に転じている。【ひと目でわかる】米中間選挙の情勢上院選の野党民主党候補ジェームズ・タラリコ州下院議員（37）が、共和党のケン・パクストン州司法長官（63）をしのぐ勢いで支持を拡大。民主党は同州の上院選で38年ぶりとなる勝利を引き寄せ、上院の過半数奪取につなげたい考えだ。◇原点は「教室」中部サンアントニオ中心部のヒスパニック（中南米系）市民集住地区に、今年に入り学区の財政難で閉校した中学校がある。「教室での経験」を政治活動の原点とするタラリコ氏が、教員養成・派遣に当たる非営利団体を通じ2011年から2年間、教員として勤務した学校だ。同団体幹部だったローラ・ルナ氏（43）は、当時大学生だったタラリコ氏の選考面接を担当した。同氏が模擬授業で三本脚の椅子を使い、「脚がそろっていなければ倒れてしまう。三権がそれぞれ強固で、連携していく必要がある」と説明したことを覚えている。「いつか選挙で選ばれる公職者になると思った。そうしたカリスマ性があった」と振り返る。◇ヒスパニック奪還課題キリスト教の神学生でもあり、保守層に響く聖書の言葉を引用して政治を語るタラリコ氏の強みは、「党派を超えて訴え掛ける」（ルナ氏）伝達力だ。タラリコ氏は、民主党幹部の応援を受けずに地域密着の選挙戦を展開。24年大統領選で景気回復に期待してトランプ大統領に投票したヒスパニック有権者の奪還を期す。「民主党員でも共和党員でもなく、テキサス州民として団結し、最も腐敗した政治家を打ち負かせば、腐敗した制度全体も倒すことができる」。タラリコ氏は10月25日、ヒスパニックが住民の約9割を占める州南部の国境の街ウェスラコで開かれた集会で、献金者への便宜供与などを巡り弾劾訴追されたパクストン氏（弾劾裁判で無罪）を批判した。大学生のフェイス・ゴンザレスさん（24）は「タラリコが民主党員だから票を投じるというわけではない」と説明。同行していた保険販売員フアン・コントレラスさん（23）が「彼自身、自分がどの政党に属しているかは関係ないと言っている。そういうところが気に入っているんだ」と補った。◇穏健保守層の離反守勢に回るパクストン氏が頼むのは、「外」からの支援だ。共和党は9月に党大会をダラスで開催。大会後もトランプ氏が応援演説で計3回、テキサス入りした。トランプ氏に近い富豪イーロン・マスク氏も、関連政治団体を通じ2億ドル（約315億円）近い資金を投入した。「この選挙戦で、何年にもわたって誰が上院を支配するかが決まる可能性がある」。パクストン氏は23日、サンアントニオ近郊のダンスホールで開いた集会でタラリコ氏を「過激派」だと断じ、危機感をあおった。聴衆には、年配のトランプ氏支持者の姿が目立つ。無職のネーサン・ケーンさん（66）は「良い仕事をしている」とトランプ氏を評価し、「民主党が体現するものが嫌いだ」と話した。ただ、トランプ氏の後ろ盾を得て予備選で伝統的保守派の現職ジョン・コーニン氏を退け、候補の座を射止めたパクストン氏には、穏健保守層の離反という不安が付きまとう。ブッシュ（子）元大統領の弟ニール氏は、タラリコ氏支持を表明。元政府職員ジャック・ニューネスさん（63）は集会の場で、「コーニンだったら勝利は確実なはずだった」と漏らした。

title: 教皇が米中間選挙に投票 史上初
body: 【ローマ共同】ローマ教皇庁（バチカン）は30日、米国籍を持つ教皇レオ14世が11月3日の米中間選挙で郵便投票を行ったと発表した。レオ14世は昨年、米国出身者として初めて教皇に選出された。在任中の教皇による米国の選挙での投票はこれまで例がなかった。投票先は明らかにされていない。発表によると、有権者登録している出身地の中西部イリノイ州シカゴでの投票を郵便で行った。レオ14世は教皇就任前に南米ペルーで長く活動したが、その間も可能な限り選挙権を行使した。市民として民主主義に参加する権利と義務への信念を抱いているという。レオ14世はこれまで移民政策やイラン情勢、人工知能（AI）を巡りトランプ大統領とたびたび対立。トランプ氏からの批判にも動じず、反論している。

title: イスラエル 与野党過半数届かず
body:
【エルサレム＝福島利之、村上愛衣】イスラエルの総選挙（定数１２０）で、選挙管理委員会が２９日に発表した開票結果では、与野党ともに過半数に届かなかった。今後、イツハク・ヘルツォグ大統領が連立政権を樹立できる可能性の高い当選者に組閣を指示するが、組閣の難航は必至だ。【図解】イスラエルの首相選出の流れ
選管の発表によると、ベンヤミン・ネタニヤフ首相の与党陣営は５３議席（過半数６１）、政権交代を目指す野党陣営は４８議席だった。
最終的な結果は１１月４日に公表される。この後、ヘルツォグ大統領が各党の代表者と協議し、１週間以内に「首相候補」に組閣を要請する。候補は４週間以内の組閣が求められ、この期間は２週間まで延長できる。
期間内の組閣に失敗した場合、大統領は別の候補に組閣を要請する。次の候補も政権を樹立できない場合、再選挙の可能性が浮上する。新政権樹立まではネタニヤフ氏が首相を続ける。ヘルツォグ氏は２８日、「再選挙を避けるためにできる限りのことをしなくてはならない」と訴えた。
選管の発表によると、与党陣営は、ネタニヤフ氏が率いる右派リクードが２７議席で最大政党となった。ユダヤ教超正統派２党は１３議席、極右２党は１３議席となった。
野党陣営は、ガディ・アイゼンコット元軍参謀総長が率いる中道ヤシャルが２１議席、中道ベヤハドが１２議席、左派民主党が８議席、右派「我が家イスラエル」は７議席で続いた。
アラブ系２政党は１９議席を獲得し躍進した。パレスチナ自治区ガザなどでの戦闘を受け、人口の２割を占めるアラブ系住民の投票率が上がった。アラブ系政党と野党陣営が組めば政権樹立につながるが、野党陣営にはアラブ系政党に拒否感が強い政党もあり、先行きは見通せない。

title: 露の独立系紙が活動停止 当局弾圧
body: ロシアでウクライナ侵攻に批判的立場を取る独立系紙「ノーバヤ・ガゼータ」が30日、「われわれは殺された」と題した声明を出し、活動停止を発表した。【地図で見る】ウクライナ戦況マップ同紙の編集長だったドミトリー・ムラトフ氏は2021年、ノーベル平和賞を受賞している。声明などによると、同紙は11月9日に活動を停止する。「ロシアの当局と情報機関が編集部を活動停止に追い込んだ」と理由を説明。モスクワにある編集部の立ち退きを求める書面が届いた上、読者からの寄付を受け取るシステムも停止され、「資金を完全に奪われた」という。同紙は1993年創刊。プーチン政権や南部チェチェン共和国の独裁体制に厳しい報道姿勢を貫いてきた。一方、2006年にはアンナ・ポリトコフスカヤ記者が射殺されるなど、これまでに6人が命を奪われた。

title: キオクシア 4-12月純利益24倍予想
body: Kentaro Okasaka[東京 ３０日 ロイター] - キオクシアホールディングスは３０日、１株９０円の中間配当を決定したと発表した。ＡＩ（人工知能）関連需要の追い風が吹く中、‌配当は２０２４年末の上場以来初。河村芳彦副社長は、累進配当を⁠基本とし、期末配当は中間配当を上回る水準とする方針を示した。２６年４─１２月期の連結純利益（国際会計基準）が前年比約２４倍の３兆５５７８億円になるとの見​通しも発表した。同社は四半期先の業績予想を開示する一方、通期見通しは公表していない。ＩＢＥＳがまとめたアナリスト１７人のコン‌センサス予想では、２７年３月期の連結純利益の平均値は５兆５８００億円。配当開始を決めたのは、ＡＩ関連需要の拡大などを背景とした事業環境の改善で、業績やキャッシュ‌フローが大きく改善したため。‌財務健全性が高まっている状況を踏まえ、事​業成長に向けた投資を継続しながら株主還元を実施できる環境が整ったと判断し‌た。河村副社長は決算説明会で、余剰キャッシュの１００％株主還元を目指す方針を示し、当面は機動的に実施‌可能な自社株買いを中心と​しつつ配当も出していく形になると述べた。２７年３月期の第２・四‌半期（２６年７－９月）の売上収益は、前四半期比で７１２９億円増となる２兆４８００億円と好調だった。生成ＡＩ用途を中心としたデ⁠ータセンター向け需要が旺盛に推移し、平均販売単価が大幅に上昇。記憶容量ベースの出荷量も増加した。アプリケーション別では、ＳＳＤ（ソリッドステートドライブ）＆ストレー⁠ジの売上収益が同４４１３億円増の１兆６１６０億円、スマートデバイスの売上​収益は同２６３２億円増の７８８９億円だった。河村‌副社長は、２７年の生産能力は全て割り振り済みと説明。２８年もスマートフォンやパソコン向けの需要軟化を法人向け需要が吸収して旺盛な需要成長を見込むとし「明⁠らかに（需要の波を超えて長期的に好況が続く）スーパーサイ⁠クルに入っている」と語った。連結子会社で岩手・北上工場を運営するキオクシア岩⁠手を来年４月１日付で吸収合併することも発表した。ＡＩデータセンター向けの旺盛な需要を背景にフラッ‌シュメモ⁠リー市場の中長期的な拡大が見込まれる中、最先端製品の製造​力の強化を図り、持続的成長を実現する目的。北上工場では２９年度中に第３製造棟が稼働開始する予定。

title: 中国産オクラ 相次ぎ基準超え農薬
body:
厚生労働省は３０日、輸入された中国産オクラから基準値を上回る農薬「メピコートクロリド」が相次いで検出されたとして、食品衛生法に基づく検査命令を出した。今後、中国産オクラ（加工品を含む）を輸入する際には、農薬の残留検査が義務づけられる。【写真】水産物を「日本からの輸入品ではない」と表示する中国のスーパー
同省によると、輸入された冷凍オクラから基準値（０・０１ｐｐｍ）を超えるメピコートクロリドを検出した事例が９～１０月に全国で３件あった。いずれも市場には流通していない。
中国産オクラの輸入量は年間１万トン前後で、農薬の検査命令は初という。

title: ジャングリア 出資に数社が関心
body:
昨年７月に開業したテーマパーク「ジャングリア沖縄」を運営するジャパンエンターテイメントは３０日、２０２６年６月期決算を発表し、売上高は１０３億円、最終利益は８９億円の赤字だった。資金繰りの悪化から同社は新規の出資者を探している。関係者によると数社が関心を示しており、来年２月の出資決定を目指している。【写真】上空から見たジャングリア沖縄
同社は売上高や利益などの目標を開示していないが、入場者数は併設の温浴施設を含めて９５万人にとどまり、目標を大幅に下回ったとみられる。
新規出資者について、加藤健史・最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）は記者会見で「数か月から半年で（決定したい）」と語った。加藤氏は、２７年６月期の入場者数の見通しを６３万人とし、人員の適正化や外部委託の削減などの構造改革で収益改善を目指すとした。
一方、オリオンビールなど沖縄県の地元企業が出資する親会社「ジャパンエンターテイメントホールディングス（ＨＤ）」は同日、定時株主総会の継続会を開催した。ジャングリアの開業を主導したコンサルタント会社「刀」の森岡毅氏は終了後の報道陣の取材に、「真摯（しんし）な話し合いをさせてもらった。前向きに動かしていく」と述べた。

title: 神戸の「モザイク」全面改装へ
body: 神戸ハーバーランドの商業施設ｕｍｉｅ（ウミエ、神戸市中央区）のうち、海に面する集合店舗ゾーン「モザイク」が全面改装されることが分かった。来年２月から一時閉館し、２０３０年前後の再開を目指す。隣接する神戸アンパンマンこどもミュージアム＆モールと観覧車は営業を続ける。港町・神戸を代表するウオーターフロントの景観をかたちづくる施設の一つが、開業から３４年を経て生まれ変わる。（長尾亮太、末永陽子）【動画】ミナト神戸が「ミッフィーの街」にモザイクは１９９２年、関西のウオーターフロント開発の先駆けとしてまち開きしたハーバーランドで、神戸港の岸壁沿いに開業した。３層構造の建物に飲食、物販店が軒を連ね、神戸ポートタワーなど港の風景を一望しながら回遊できるスポットとして人気を呼んだ。もともと三菱倉庫（東京）の倉庫跡地で、当初は同社と現在の阪急阪神東宝グループが共同出資する会社が運営。フェリー発着地としての機能も担っていた。１２年には隣接する百貨店「神戸阪急」が閉店。１３年から旧神戸阪急と旧Ｈａ・Ｒｅ（ハレ）の商業ビル２棟にモザイクを加えた一帯をウミエと名付け、イオンモール（千葉市）が一体運営を始めた。同年にアンパンマンこどもミュージアムが開業するなど、子育て中のファミリー層に照準を合わせた取り組みが実を結び、にぎわいを取り戻した。インバウンド（訪日客）や地元住民も含め、ウミエ全体で年間１７００万人（２５年度）の客が訪れる。今回のモザイク改装は、施設や設備の老朽化に伴って進められる。空調用配管からの水漏れなどが起き、建材として多用する木の腐食も進んでいた。海辺で憩える機能の向上などを図るとみられる。現在、約８０店が営業している。複数の出店事業者などによると、すでに改装の方針が伝わり、対応を検討しているという。神戸のウオーターフロントでは、新港突堤にアリーナや劇場型水族館ができるなど新たなにぎわいづくりが進んでおり、モザイクの今後の運営にも関心が集まる。

title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
summary: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.
body:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.

G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when theUS eased sanctions on Russiaas part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time forUkraine to get a new leaderto strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meetingEuropean diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrovby refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He saidRussia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July,Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots- three weeks after offering the country such a right.

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
summary: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.
body:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
In a later update, the firm set it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
summary: It is Pike's first public statement since she survived an execution attempt by lethal injection in September.
body:
The BBC's Ione Wells looks at what Christa Pike says in her statement about surviving a botched execution.
US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in the statement.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.
Christa Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbita
She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Pike is thought to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.
I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
I interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about her
What happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive?
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said in her statement on Friday. "But healing is not the same as being okay."
Her lawyers previously said she had suffered from pneumonia following the attempted execution, had significant swelling on her arms and was also unable to swallow.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and Shipp
Pike's botched execution captivated and shocked the world last month and shocked Pike, too.
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said in her statement.
Bethany Mann, a friend of Pike's and a founder of Child Arise Tennessee, which supports children and families affected by parental incarceration, told the BBC on Friday that she had been in direct contact with Pike since the botched execution attempt.
When asked about her reaction to Pike's statement, Mann said: "Truthfully, I don't know that I have anything to add to what Christa has already expressed so powerfully herself, and I want to be respectful of her privacy."
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".
Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.
Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."
She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess".
She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology.
"All I wanted was justice," Martinez said.
Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.

title: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
summary: Hundreds of people are also understood to have stayed in the front-line town, despite the dangers.
body:
Watch: How will the evacuation of Oleshky unfold?
Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed the evacuees were on their way to southern Russia, from where they will travel on to Ukraine through Belarus.
Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".
Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".
A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.
Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.
"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."
Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.
Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.
Oleshky residents had a four-hour window to board buses to be evacuated to either Russia or Ukraine
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Residents travelled from Oleshky in convoy to Armyansk in Russian-occupied Crimea
Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.
In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."
Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova spoke to journalists before arriving in Oleshky
The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.
On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.
A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.
Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
summary: The escalation came after the government suspended two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.
body:
Officers were faced down by critics of the move outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
Bogdan Święczkowski appeared before reporters near the court's building
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk have been involved in a political tug-of-war over the court
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski  to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
body:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday,taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market valueafter it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

title: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack

body:
Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, has been hit by a $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack - thought to be the biggest in history.
Half of the assets have been frozen but many remain in the hands of the hackers, the cryptocurrency giant said. It later added that it has "begun recovering" some funds.
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit, though no one has claimed responsibility. Binance did not directly respond to questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea.

title: City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
summary: Ian Thomas, who heads the City of London Corporation, tops the Black Powerlist in its 21st year.
body:
Ian Thomas, chief executive of the City of London Corporation, has been named the UK's most influential Black Briton in this year's Black Powerlist awards.
The 57-year old is the first Black person to oversee the Square Mile's governing body in its more than 900-year history.
The City of London Corporation is an administrative body with responsibility for London's central financial district, headed by its own Lord Mayor.
Thomas tops the 2027 Black Powerlist, which recognises the most powerful people of African and Caribbean heritage in the UK.
The award body said he was "a respected public-service leader with over 30 years' experience in local government".
Other influential names in this year's top ten include entrepreneurs Emma Grede and Steven Bartlett, as well as actor and filmmaker Sir Idris Elba.
Comedian Sir Lenny Henry has also been recognised, with a Lifetime Achievement award, for co-founding Comic Relief, which has raised over £1.6bn since 1985.
Now in its 21st year, the Black Powerlist celebrates people who have broken through barriers to reach leadership roles, thereby inspiring future generations.
"It exists to show young people of African and Caribbean heritage what is possible, in fields they might never have considered," said Michael Eboda, the list's publisher.
Sir Lenny Henry is being honoured with a Lifetime Achievement Award
Thomas said he secured the role at the head of the City of London Corporation in 2022 only following seven interviews and an election.
'When I started my journey in public service, I never, ever thought, [not] in a million years, that I'd be recognised in this way," he told the BBC.
As chief executive, he oversees around 5,000 staff with responsibilities including the City of London Police, 11,000 acres of open spaces such as Epping Forest and Hampstead Heath, and advocacy for the UK's financial and professional services sector.
Thomas was born in Sheffield to parents who made the city their home after leaving Jamaica as part of the Windrush generation.
"They worked incredibly hard and instilled that sense of discipline and respect, and that's the core of how I do business," he said of his upbringing.
Growing up, Thomas aspired to be a footballer and took part in trials alongside Alan Shearer.
Reflecting on his own change of direction, Thomas joked it was about "following dreams and if they don't come true… there's always something else".
Before joining the City of London Corporation, Thomas served as chief executive of the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames where he oversaw public services and a £1.2bn regeneration programme.
He was appointed a CBE in the 2019 New Year Honours in the wake of the Rotherham Abuse scandal for transforming children's services during his time as strategic director for children and young people at Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council.
Thomas replaces last year's incumbent, Afua Kyei, the Bank of England's chief financial officer and executive director, and is joined on this year's list by Comfort Ero, the President and chief executive of the International Crisis Group, who takes second place.

title: How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant
summary: The retail giant - which started life at a Wolverhampton market - is now at threat of collapse.
body:
Poundland has been a recognisable presence on high streets for more than 35 years
"When I told people what I wanted to do, open shops on the high street selling things for one pound, they said, 'how will you find products to sell for a pound, what about inflation, it will never work.'"
That is how Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, describes the genesis of the budget giant - which went on to employ thousands of people and see over a million customers a week -on his own website,external.
But now the West Midlands-based retailer is teetering on the edge, after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group.
Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators
Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis
Having spent time on his parents stall since the age of two Wolverhampton-born businessman Smith started out in the very same place - selling items for £1 from his own stall.
After a £50,000 loan from his parents he opened the first Poundland shop, in The Octagon Shopping Centre in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, on 13 December 1990.
That first day, with a range of 624 products, the store took more than £13,000 - "and Poundland was born," Smith said.
Smith and his wife, Tracy, now based in Shropshire, owned the company for 16 years.
In 2006, he decided the time had come and he sold his final shares in the business for £250m, but later said the sale felt it was "as though somebody had died".
Steven Smith founded Poundland in 1990 with the help of his father, Kevin Smith
But by 2025,the Walsall-based company was itself sold for just £1.
Its owner, Polish firm Pepco, confirmed it had sold the brand for a "nominal" sum to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.
At the time Poundland had more than 800 stores across the UK and Ireland and employed around 16,000 staff.
"I did pick up the phone when I heard it was for sale but I was a bit too late," Smith said after the sale.
Now, the retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
A protest was held outside the Poundland HQ on Thursday, Claire Sutcliffe - who has been at the company for nearly a decade - among those demonstrating.
Sutcliffe said she was "very sad" to hear the news
Questioned about how she felt, the 49-year-old replied she was "very sad", adding: "Nine years is a lot working for Poundland and they've been really good to me as a Poundland family, really supportive."
Sutcliffe added that some had worked for the business for 20 years and "it's just very sad for us all".
Asked what her message was to owners Gordon Brothers, she replied: "Please just sell.
"Save our jobs, we've all got families to feed and it's... near Christmas."
About 25 people took part in a protest at Poundland in Walsall on Thursday
Professor Sarah Montano, a retail expert from the University of Birmingham, said: "The real problem for Poundland is, when they first started it was really great because everything was £1, that was a really unique selling point for them.
"[Today] there's competitors which are offering very similar prices and for quite a lot of products they're offering them cheaper."
She added that some competitors had "really got their finger on the key trends".
In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".
"The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs," they said.
"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."
They also thanked "staff, suppliers and customers for their continued support".

title: Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials
summary: The prime minister has categorically ruled out an early general election, but it has not stopped speculation at Westminster.
body:
Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has nearly three years to go before he has to call an election and he has repeatedly and categorically ruled out going to the country early.
But the discussion persists - and many think it is a real possibility.
After Wednesday's Budget, that talk has only increased.
As one former Labour minister puts it: "Why would you sprinkle round a few politically smart (albeit small) giveaways now but delay all the really tough and unpopular decisions on welfare anddefenceto an autumn spending review if you weren't creating a window for a spring election?"
Others have also suggested to the BBC that Chancellor John Healey's plans felt like a pre-election programme.
They argue the Budget contained voter-friendly measures on the cost of living, such as£100 help for many with energy billsand extending VAT cuts on electricity bills. Young voters are to be offered help on to the housing ladder, through theYour First Home scheme.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has questioned why some-voter friendly measures announced by Healey will only be in place until the summer.
Could it be, she suggests, that the prime minister plans to go to the country before these measures run out?
(The counter-argument to this is that household energy pressures are less severe in the summer.)
Some MPs also point out the prime minister is popular at the moment and Labour is leading in most polls.
Reform, who had led the polls for some time, have had a difficult few months.
Will things ever look better for Burnham, they ask.
Andy Burnham arrives to vote in July's Greater Manchester mayoral elections
Then there are the difficult spending decisions faced by the chancellor.
How to find the money to fund an increase in defence spending? How to bring down the welfare bill? How to cut departmental spending to make the books add up?
"He is delaying all of the bad stuff until after a poll," reckons one Conservative MP.
The Liberal Democrats have claimed there is a 30% chance of a general election on 10 December. The party has been put on a "snap election footing".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said he thinks there could be a general election in May.
It is worth pointing out predictions of an early election are coming more from opposition MPs, some of whom might be keen to cause a bit of trouble.
An election has to be held by August 2029, but some Labour MPs have said they are so convinced an early election is on the way that they have told their staff to prepare for one in the first half of next year.
Burnham was a member of Gordon Brown's losing team in 2010
Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
Analysis: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
There are, though, plenty of arguments against a general election in the next year.
Firstly, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out in interviews.
On Wednesday, he saidexplicitly that there would not be an election in the next 12 months. Politicians can change their minds, but one veteran Tory concludes a change of heart, after emphatic denials, would be too damaging to "Brand Burnham".
Next – despite the chancellor's giveaways on the cost of living – theoverall economic outlookis "pretty grim", in the words of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Real Household Disposable Income looks set to fall in the coming months. Interest rates are predicted to go up. Nobody knows for sure what will happen next in the Middle East – and whether things could get worse before they get better.
Burnham has pledged a rewiring of the British state. He plans to set out a 10-year plan in the coming weeks. But without more detail, some wonder if voters will know enough to make a judgement.
On more than one occasion, Burnham has vowed to bring about the most significant change in British politics in four decades.
One former Labour minister could not detect much in this week's Budget to that effect, saying: "It's not an end to 40 years of neoliberalism is it?"
That message was echoed by another Labour MP: "It was too low key to be an election Budget."
"It was a disappointment, a play it safe, keep everything ticking over Budget… crumbs for all," said another.
"No early general election after that Budget. We would be toast."
Theresa May, pictured here with husband Philip, decided to call a snap election while on a walking holiday
Some argue Burnham would benefit from having his own mandate, with his own manifesto. But given the size of Labour's general election win last time, many MPs think it's inevitable that Labour will lose ground.
Others say that if Burnham's government does feel the need to break Sir Keir Starmer's manifesto commitments by increasing taxes, they should just do it, instead of holding an election.
"If we need an election to put up taxes then arguably that's easier to do now with our massive majority than to start an election campaign on the basis that we're calling it in order to put up taxes," said one Labour MP.
"People act like a manifesto is a legal document written in blood. Plenty of governments have broken lots of manifesto promises."
Remember too that the prime minister has promised a detailed plan on social care in England, which is some way off. He has also not decided how far he wants to go in taking the UK closer to the EU.
There is a lot for Number 10 to weigh up.
Labour might look back to Gordon Brown, whodid not call an early electionwhen he was prime minister and doing well in the polls. If he had gone to the country in October 2007, might Labour have stayed in power?
But there will be plenty of others who look to Theresa May. Sheopted for a snap general electionin April 2017, after mulling the decision over on a walking holiday in Wales. Despite flying high in the polls, the Tories lost their majority.
So will Burnham do it?
He might be tempted. But there are plenty of risks that mean it would be far from an easy choice.

title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
summary: The meeting involved representatives from the UK's four nations to discuss devolving more powers to regions and cities.
body:
Andy Burnham met the first ministers from Scotland and Wales and representatives from Northern Ireland in Glasgow
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.
SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".
Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.
Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham
Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM
Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".
"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.
"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid thepolitical fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute.
Burnham held talks with first ministers John Swinney (left) and Rhun ap Iowerth (right)
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.
He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".
In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.
Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.
The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".
Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.
He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.
The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.
John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.
"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.
"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."
A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.
Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.
"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."
He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.
The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.
A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
summary: The government is under pressure to set out a path to greater defence spending, as ministers unveil plans to boost UK firms.
body:
Wes Streeting has defended the government's current approach
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather thanannounced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments tocut their capital budgets by 1%.
Labour MP Tan Dhesi has led the latest criticism of government defence spending
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and theNato-wide target of 3.5%by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.
Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'

title: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
summary: The new government office in Manchester has launched 50 job adverts for roles including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
body:
Andy Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as PM
Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.
The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove toBurnham's aim to devolve poweracross the country.
Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.
The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".
There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.
The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.
BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.
No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.
Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit...  shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".
The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".
No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.
No10 North is designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - with a replica black door inside on show
Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.
It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.
No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.
Burnham made opening No10 Northone of his first acts as prime minister, describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.
No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims andcalled for a "mindset shift"across the UK's central government.
Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.
"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."
Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministerstold him they could not revealfigures on headcounts and office attendance.
According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.
Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiledcontroversial powers for mayors in Englandto charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.
It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

title: Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
summary: The Tory Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he's working on what he's calling a "tax rebate scheme".
body:
English mayors - such as those pictured here - are getting more control over funding
English regional mayors due to be handed a share of tax revenues by central government will be free to use it to give cash grants to individual residents and businesses, it has emerged.
In his Budget, Chancellor John Healey unveiled plans to allow mayors to keep some cash from income tax and business rates collected locally, describing it as "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants local leaders to be given more control over how money is spent in their areas to boost economic growth and services.
But Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he has been given assurances that he will be able to give grants to local residents instead.
Lord Houchen told the BBC he is working on a voluntary scheme that would give local residents the opportunity to apply for a share of the tax distributed to his region.
He said Treasury officials had told him this would be acceptable within the government's rules around the devolution of funding.
"It's a technical point around spending decisions," Lord Houchen told the BBC.
He said devolution of funding was a "good thing" and "means mayors are able to decide spending commitments, which includes rebates".
The BBC has been told mayors could choose to use the tax revenues they received from the government to offer grants to individual residents or businesses.
But any mayor who decided to use the money in this way would have less for other local priorities, such as housing and transport.
Lord Houchen has described his proposal as a "tax rebate scheme".
The Treasury would regard these payments as grants, because His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is the only government authority in the UK that can issue income tax rebates.
Most of England's 14 strategic authorities are led by Labour mayors who have welcomed the move to give them a portion of income tax receipts.
Sources close to Reform UK's Greater Lincolnshire Mayor Andrea Jenkyns, and her counterpart in Hull and East Yorkshire, Luke Campbell, say they are waiting for more details to fully understand how they could use these tax revenues to benefit their regions.
Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Lord Houchen says fiscal devolution is a "good thing"
The governmentpublished its broad approach,externalto reforming funding for local and regional government in England after Wednesday's Budget.
As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding from ring-fenced grants, allocated by central government to be spent on specific policy areas.
From April 2028, all mayors of strategic authorities in England will be assigned a share of basic-rate income tax generated in their areas.
Each mayor will receive a bespoke funding allocation that takes into account regional inequalities in tax bases, with the exact amounts to be set at the government's spending review next year.
"The government is not devolving the power to set income tax rates or thresholds to mayors but will be granting significantly more flexibility as to how assigned revenues are spent locally," the government's plan says.
"Mayors will be able to choose where to target funding, for example whether to maintain funding for local transport or prioritise other interventions."
From next year, mayors will also receive a 20% share of locally retained business rates.
This will be the first step towards allowing local and mayoral authorities to retain 100% of their business rates income before the end of the decade.
From 2028, strategic authorities led by mayors will also be given the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, often dubbed a "tourist tax".
This charge will be an uncapped levy as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.
Labour mayors in 10 city regions saidthey would voluntarily limit the charge to 5%, but others - such as Lord Houchen - said they would not introduce the levy.
Burnham - who used to be a mayor himself in Greater Manchester - argues that funding and decision-making powers are too centralised in the UK.
The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7,according to the OECD,external, a global policy forum.
That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).
But critics of fiscal devolution raise concerns about local capability, and inequalities between areas.
The Centre for Cities think tank says some areas may not have the expertise to manage developed powers effectively, risking deeper economic inequalities between areas.
The think tank supports fiscal devolution and believes it can offer significant benefits, if the challenges are managed effectively.
The Tees Valley Combined Authority (TVCA) led by Lord Houchen isfacing a government inspectioninto its finances, after Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said he had concerns about its "long-term financial sustainability".
The authority said it welcomed the scrutiny and would continue to make improvements where needed.
